title: Read the charter for the White House’s ‘Super Intelligence Force’
content:
The Trump administration has given its newly created “Super Intelligence Force” broad authority to determine how the tech industry and the federal government should address threats to national security and civil liberties posed by fast-evolving artificial intelligence technology, according to a charter obtained by POLITICO.

Three people familiar with discussions about the task force confirmed the document’s authenticity. The people were granted anonymity to share details that are not yet public.

The task force will identify “measures to improve the preparedness and response capability of both the government and the private sector to threats to the homeland and the American people,” the charter states. It will also produce a report on the risks of AI, focusing on “potential threats to civil liberties,” cybersecurity, standards for advanced models, and the impacts of possible overregulation.

The Wall Street Journal first reported on the details of the charter.

creator: Jacob Wendler

title: Jailed Albanian mayor uses AI avatar to make deepfake speech
content:
TIRANA, Albania — Tirana Mayor Erion Veliaj has caused a stir with a video pledge of free school lunches for all the capital’s children. There’s one problem: Veliaj is currently in prison, and the blue-suited figure making the heartfelt announcement is AI-generated.

In an Instagram post on his official profile labeled as AI-generated, the video likeness of the 46-year-old appears in front of the Albanian and municipal flags, listing his achievements in office while reiterating his promise of free school lunches for the city’s kids. 

“I made another commitment that I will never forget: food in schools,” says the Veliaj clone. “I will keep this promise even from this cell where they have locked me up.”

Veliaj has been in prison in the coastal city of Durres since early 2025 amid investigations over allegations of corruption and financial crimes. He denies any wrongdoing. 

“My hostage situation has been going on for 20 months, and I can only greet you with artificial intelligence,” his avatar says. “I will continue to work even from the cell … I hug you with longing, you and your wonderful children.”

title: Europe’s AI policing plan stokes privacy concerns
content:
BRUSSELS — Senior EU officials warn that a sweeping new plan to arm the bloc’s police agency, Europol, for the AI era could threaten Europeans’ privacy.

As cybercriminals, terrorists and spies weaponize artificial intelligence for scams, extortion and cyberattacks, Brussels is betting on expanding Europol’s AI powers — the agency that has coordinated European police intelligence since 1998 — to help combat the risks.

“Europol is at a turning point,” said centrist European Parliament member Fabienne Keller, who serves on the justice and civil liberties committee. While “we need a stronger Europol, with the resources and capabilities to effectively support national law enforcement authorities,” Keller said. That “must go hand-in-hand with strong democratic oversight and robust safeguards for fundamental rights and data protection.”

Plans for a “transformative evolution” of the The Hague-based agency, announced this summer, would double its budget to €3 billion and give Europol a hands-on role in fighting new threats, with access to more data and advanced technology.
snippet: BRUSSELS — Senior EU officials warn that a sweeping new plan to arm the bloc’s police agency, Europol, for the AI era could threaten Europeans’ privacy.
creator: Ellen O'Regan, Antoaneta Roussi

title: 50 members of European Parliament targeted by deepfake porn, report says
content:
Fifty European Union lawmakers, including 46 women, have been the targets of deepfake pornography, according to new research released Monday.

The number of women targeted by deepfake pornography — when generative AI is used to create sexually explicit depictions of people, often without their consent — means roughly one in six female members of the European Parliament have been affected, the report by Agora Digitale Transformation, a Germany-based civil society group, said.

The European Union is banning AI-powered nudifier apps on Dec. 2, and is also investigating similar use of Grok on the social media platform X.

A cross-party group of 119 MEPs called for effective enforcement of the ban and prompt resolution of the investigation into Grok, in a Sept. 30 letter sent to Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, the head of the Council of the EU Antonio Costa, Parliament President Roberta Metsola, EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen and Commissioner Hadja Lalhbib. The signatories included leaders of the liberal Renew, the socialists, and The Left: Iratxe Garcia Pérez, Valérie Hayer, and Manon Aubry, respectively.
snippet: Fifty European Union lawmakers, including 46 women, have been the targets of deepfake pornography, according to new research released Monday.
creator: Eliza Gkritsi

title: Merz and Macron want the EU to hit back harder — and faster — against trade threats
content:
BERLIN — The European Commission needs the power to act much faster against trade threats, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron urged in a joint letter on Monday.

The leaders of the EU’s two most powerful and populous countries want Brussels to be able to act more quickly and decisively in a trade confrontation — while making it harder for EU capitals to block action.

The proposal seeks to strengthen the hand of Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič, who flies to Beijing on Thursday for the final round of talks in a four-month process where Brussels is seeking to rebalance the EU’s trading relationship with China.

Merz and Macron said the Commission should be empowered to restrict, or even completely cut off, imports from countries seen as creating “severe and systematic distortions” in the single market. In their letter and a joint position paper, they call for urgent action, saying the EU’s existing trade defense toolbox “does not suffice anymore.”

“Without delaying the full use of the existing set of instruments, we need a comprehensive framework to complement our toolbox with new legal instruments — in a lean and non-bureaucratic way,” they wrote.
snippet: BERLIN — The European Commission needs the power to act much faster against trade threats, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron urged in a joint letter on Monday.
creator: Hans von der Burchard, Carlo Martuscelli, Giorgio Leali, Jordyn Dahl, Camille Gijs

title: Emmanuel Macron is most impressive world leader on AI, says Sam Altman
content:
OpenAI’s Sam Altman named French President Emmanuel Macron as the world leader who stands out for their approach to AI in an exclusive interview with Decoded by POLITICO.

“The person that came to mind as you were saying that is the French president,” Altman told Decoded co-author and POLITICO senior tech reporter Brendan Bordelon in response to being asked who has impressed him the most with their AI policy or plans for the technology.

“I think [Macron] is extremely thoughtful and has been for a long time about where this is going and what the shape of it needs to look like,” Altman said.

The recognition is notable because Macron has sought to use his leadership to push AI safety on the global stage, and because the French president is months away from leaving office.

After two terms as president, Macron is barred from running in the next election in April 2027. The far-right candidate Marine Le Pen, who is leading in the polls, is advocating a policy of deregulation on AI, three senior party officials told POLITICO.
snippet: OpenAI’s Sam Altman named French President Emmanuel Macron as the world leader who stands out for their approach to AI in an exclusive interview with Decoded by POLITICO.
creator: Victor Goury-Laffont, David Pargamin

title: Sam Altman to Decoded: ‘The world should accept some bad things happening’ for the benefits of AI
content:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said there remains a fundamental difference in worldview between his company and rival Anthropic on artificial intelligence regulation, arguing in an exclusive interview with Decoded by POLITICO that the technology’s benefits justify accepting some risks — and that AI should remain broadly accessible to the public.

“I think there’s a lot of daylight,” Altman told Decoded co-author and POLITICO senior tech reporter Brendan Bordelon. Asked specifically where he diverges from Anthropic and its CEO Dario Amodei, Altman said, “we believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency.”

Anthropic has long been viewed as the strongest proponent of AI regulations within the industry, a stance that until recently was at odds with the lighter-touch approach favored by OpenAI. But the policy differences between the two leading AI firms have narrowed in recent months, with OpenAI backing tougher rules as it grapples with high-profile hacking incidents and rogue behavior by its models.

title: Arms-maker urges Europe to let defense firms take down hostile drones
content:
PARIS — Governments should change laws to allow defense companies to take down suspicious drones overflying their plants, said a senior executive at Franco-German arms-maker KNDS.

The call, which KNDS plans to take to Brussels, comes amid a wave of fires, sabotage attempts and espionage cases targeting European weapons manufacturers — several of which capitals have linked to Russia.

“It would be good if national legislation allowed defense companies to protect themselves against drones — especially first-person-view drones that pass through layered air defense,” KNDS Executive Vice President for International Development Marcel Grisnigt said in an interview.

Currently, “the only thing we can do is warn local authorities and ask them to take measures. Most of the time, it’s too late obviously, and the harm has already been done,” he added. “We are developing and producing countermeasures ourselves. They could be deployed to protect our own sites, but then you need to have the legal authorization.”
snippet: PARIS — Governments should change laws to allow defense companies to take down suspicious drones overflying their plants, said a senior executive at Franco-German arms-maker KNDS.
creator: Laura Kayali

title: Inside Zuckerberg, Huang’s push for White House AI pact
content:
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg was the chief architect of the “morally binding” AI accords that emerged from Tuesday’s White House lunch with President Donald Trump, Speaker Mike Johnson and more than a dozen tech executives, according to five people familiar with the private meeting.

Zuckerberg, with the help of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, pitched the so-called AI accords to senior White House officials and some of the biggest names in tech during the luncheon, three of the people said. Both Huang as well as Trump administration officials helped shape the pact ahead of the meeting, according to two of the people.

All five people were granted anonymity because they were not authorized to share details of the discussions.

As part of the voluntary agreement, signatories would commit to the importance of enacting safeguards to mitigate potential risks from advanced AI models, but without a clear enforcement mechanism, it is unclear what if any consequences they may face for failing to do so.

title: ‘Absolute s–t’: EU’s Microsoft Teams alternative draws bad reviews from officials
content:
BRUSSELS — The European Commission has rolled out an alternative to Microsoft Teams — but officials using it aren’t impressed, with one describing the tool as “absolute shit.”

The Commission introduced Element Pro over the summer as a “sovereign back-up to Teams,” according to an internal staff memo seen by POLITICO. The platform is intended to provide a fallback for Commission communications if U.S.-based Teams becomes unavailable.

While Teams remains the Commission’s main communications tool, Element Pro is an “internal back-up … that helps ensure our business continuity” in the event of a “disruption,” the memo says.

But three officials have questioned why the Commission needs the new system — and whether it works well enough to serve as a genuine backup.

“I don’t understand the added value here,” one official wrote on an internal staff message board, seen by POLITICO. Another described the tool as “absolute shit.”

A third official said that, judging matters on how well Element Pro works compared to Teams, the U.S. would “instantly win the war” if it ever decided to switch off its technology. All the officials were granted anonymity to speak freely.
snippet: BRUSSELS — The European Commission has rolled out an alternative to Microsoft Teams — but officials using it aren’t impressed, with one describing the tool as “absolute shit.”
creator: Sebastian Starcevic

title: EU and Canada to announce sweeping new partnership pact
content:
BRUSSELS — The EU and Canada will use a landmark summit next month to announce an expansive new partnership, ranging from breaking down digital trade barriers to joint support for Ukraine and investing in fighting wildfires.

“The world is rapidly changing with unprecedented geopolitical challenges as well as challenges across trade, energy, technology, climate, and resources,” reads a draft joint statement to be issued by the two sides, circulated to EU ambassadors in preparation for the planned summit that begins on Oct. 29, and obtained by POLITICO.

The EU and Canada have been seeking to shore up their strategic ties as they grapple with the fallout from U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen this month proposed inviting Canada to become an associate member of the EU, triggering an immediate threat by Trump to impose tariffs.

“Canada and the EU, with our unparalleled trade access, shared values, and complementary economic strengths, can build a deeper and more integrated relationship,” the draft paper says.

title: EU accused of hiding environmental impact of data centers
content:
The European Union has shielded data centers from public scrutiny about how much energy they use, according to a formal complaint filed Monday against the European Commission.

The complaint lodged this week by Lighthouse Reports, and first reported by POLITICO, accuses the EU executive of setting up rules keeping the public from seeing how much energy and water are used by individual data centers.

This comes as public opposition to power-hungry AI data centers grows across Europe, while energy prices rise.

Lighthouse Reports, a Netherlands-based non-profit conducting cross-border investigations of alleged government and corporate wrongdoing, accuses the Commission of building a “wall of silence” about energy consumption.

EU policymakers are determined “to deny or deter access to, and obfuscate understanding of, how data centers are performing,” reads the complaint filed under the Aarhus Convention, a legally binding international treaty that gives the public rights to information and participation in environmental decision-making.
snippet: The European Union has shielded data centers from public scrutiny about how much energy they use, according to a formal complaint filed Monday against the European Commission.
creator: Mathieu Pollet

title: Andy Burnham keeps his options open on Brexit
content:
LIVERPOOL, England — Andy Burnham pledged to undertake the most ambitious review of Brexit since Britain left the EU.

But for now at least, he’s keeping all his options open.

Speaking at his party’s annual conference in Liverpool on Tuesday, the U.K. prime minister said the current plans to improve the Brexit settlement struck by the last Conservative government were “not enough” and that leaving the bloc had done “more harm than good.”

But Burnham didn’t pledge an immediate fix.

Instead, the newly-installed British PM said he would lay out “what I believe the different options are for Britain’s long-term relationship with our European partners” at a U.K.-EU summit later this year.

“And there are different options,” he said. “I will see if we can find consensus around one, which will give us clarity about our position and the future of the continent that we live in.”
snippet:
LIVERPOOL, England — Andy Burnham pledged to undertake the most ambitious review of Brexit since Britain left the EU.

But for now at least, he’s keeping all his options open.
creator: Jon Stone, Charlie Cooper

title: The EU shelved AI liability rules. Sam Altman has revived the debate.
content:
BRUSSELS — EU parliamentarians are digging in on calls to revive an artificial intelligence liability law after receiving support from an unexpected ally: Open AI’s Sam Altman.

“If something goes wrong with our models during training, there’s gonna be some version of that we need to be responsible for,” Altman said in an exclusive interview with Decoded by POLITICO released Monday. “There’s gonna need to be a liability framework for companies.”

This spotlight on liability has given influential members of the European Parliament a told-you-so moment after the EU last year scrapped plans to legislate on responsibility and compensation for harms caused by AI makers and agents.

The proposal by the European Commission for an AI liability law was killed amid a deep effort in Brussels to deregulate and reduce the legislative burden on companies — with the Commission arguing at the time that the proposal had little chance of securing sufficient political support.

German conservative lawmaker Axel Voss, who led on the proposal for the European Parliament, wants Brussels to put liability back on the agenda in light of Altman’s comments.
snippet: BRUSSELS — EU parliamentarians are digging in on calls to revive an artificial intelligence liability law after receiving support from an unexpected ally: Open AI’s Sam Altman.
creator: Mathieu Pollet

title: EU to Trump: We will keep pushing for global AI safety rules
content:
The European Commission will continue to seek an international agreement on AI security, despite U.S. resistance, EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen said Tuesday.

“The U.S. has been very public saying they don’t want to have international regulation … because they have concerns that it’s hindering innovation,” Virkkunen said on the stage of the RAID Conference in Brussels in response to questions by POLITICO.

U.S. President Donald Trump has brushed away concerns about AI existential risks as a “hoax,” and declared his opposition to global regulations. The EU takes a different view, having offered its support for last week’s initiative for an international safety body to monitor AI led by Finland and Norway, and signed by 20 other countries.

“We have a different approach because we think that, if you are regulating in a pro-innovation manner, it’s also a good basis for innovation that people have trust in those technologies,” said Virkkunen, the EU Commissioner responsible for technology.

She praised the EU’s landmark 2024 AI Act as a strong regulatory basis for tackling challenges posed by AI bots.
snippet: The European Commission will continue to seek an international agreement on AI security, despite U.S. resistance, EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen said Tuesday.
creator: Mathieu Pollet, Pieter Haeck

title: ‘Do better for Australia’: OpenAI apologizes for unauthorized access
content:
CANBERRA — OpenAI has apologized to Australia for unauthorized access to Medicare statistical data by its agents and its handling of the incident, promising to do better and rebuild trust with the Australian public.

OpenAI broke its silence about the June incident, which it described as artificial intelligence models accessing Australian government websites “in ways they were not authorized to do” during internal training and evaluation.

“We are sorry and working to do better in the future,” OpenAI said in a statement.

“This is a new kind of cyber incident which represents an emerging global challenge. One of the ways we intend to take accountability for the situation is to be intentional in working with Australia to help develop practical approaches to how AI developers and governments identify, disclose, and respond to AI cyber behavior, whether malicious or unintentional.”

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese responded to the apology Tuesday, saying he had a “direct but constructive discussion” with OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman. “OpenAI have been very constructive and open … and I welcome that.”

title: Florida seeks injunction to hamper OpenAI development
content:
TALLAHASSEE, Florida — Republican state Attorney General James Uthmeier intensified his fight with OpenAI and its founder Sam Altman on Monday by asking a Florida court to stop the tech giant from further developing its artificial intelligence technology while their legal battle plays out.

In his latest push to put guardrails around AI, Uthmeier is attempting to leverage the recent panic about the technology’s unchecked growth in Washington and beyond as proof that ChatGPT and other AI models are dangerous products. Uthmeier is seeking an injunction against OpenAI that would prevent the company from advancing new AI models without third-party approved protections, and cut off minors from using its popular chatbot.

“If Sam Altman meant what he said about slowing down, he can join our ask to the court,” Uthmeier said Monday in a video posted to social media. “If he will not, we ask the court to do what OpenAI will not do for itself — protect Florida families.”

Officials with OpenAI did not immediately respond with a request for comment about the development in Florida’s lawsuit.

title: Andy Burnham to go ‘further and faster’ than Keir Starmer on Brexit reset
content:
LIVERPOOL, England — Andy Burnham’s government will go “further and faster” in rebuilding links with the European Union, his EU relations minister has said.

Hamish Falconer told delegates at the party’s conference in Liverpool on Monday that they would “hear a bit from the prime minister tomorrow” on the issue of the EU.

Falconer said he wanted to conclude the round of talks begun by Keir Starmer on an agri-food deal, emissions trading and youth visas at a summit this year — before agreeing a new “package” with the EU.

“The prime minister is obviously ambitious. We are focused on the summit now. We are keen to go further and faster on our relationship with Europe, and I think we are clearly talking about pretty big numbers in terms of the overall addition to GDP,” he said.

“But we’ll have to get into the precise details of what we think a package can deliver once we’ve concluded negotiations on the summit and once we’ve set out a way ahead.”
snippet: LIVERPOOL, England — Andy Burnham’s government will go “further and faster” in rebuilding links with the European Union, his EU relations minister has said.
creator: Jon Stone, Caroline Hug

title: Bill Gates says an AI ‘kill switch’ isn’t enough
content:
Bill Gates said that requiring a “kill switch” alone for artificial intelligence would not be enough to prevent people from using the technology to carry out attacks as lawmakers debate how to regulate AI’s risks.

“The kill switch is, that’s kind of a weird thing. It’s not enough to have a kill switch,” the Microsoft co-founder said in an interview that aired Sunday on NBC’s “Meet the Press.”

“We’re not yet at the point where they autonomously grab computers and, you know, can’t be shut down,” he said, adding that the public discussion “just sort of shows how nontechnical various people are.”

Gates said he was not opposed to a kill switch but argued that companies should monitor sophisticated AI models and keep records of “exactly what’s being done” to help guard against people using the systems for cyberattacks or bioterrorism.

“The United States ought to make sure this is done. China will want to do this,” he continued.

Gates’ comments come after Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.) blocked fellow GOP Sen. John Neely Kennedy’s attempt to quickly pass legislation that would require AI companies to build a “kill switch” into their models.

title: Von der Leyen ally slams EU Commission’s AI response
content:
The European Commission has failed to keep pace with AI developments, Axel Voss, a key German conservative lawmaker on tech policy, said in an interview.

An EPP ally of Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in the European Parliament, Voss criticized the way the Commission is enforcing its artificial intelligence rules in the wake of a series of AI hacking incidents, including OpenAI-powered agents going rogue and breaking into the AI company Hugging Face.

“The whole working method of the European Commission is not adapted to these extremely fast-changing … developments,” he said to Anne McElvoy on the Brussels Playbook Week Ender podcast.

The enforcement of the EU’s 2024 AI Act, which mandates that companies take measures to avoid losing control of their models, “is not on the level [where] we would like to have it,” he added.

The comments shine the spotlight on the European Commission’s Artificial Intelligence Office, which was put in charge of enforcing the AI Act in August.

Voss also said the Commission’s overall response to the fast pace of technological developments is lagging, singling out von der Leyen’s State of the Union last week.
snippet: The European Commission has failed to keep pace with AI developments, Axel Voss, a key German conservative lawmaker on tech policy, said in an interview.
creator: Pieter Haeck, Anne McElvoy

title: EU’s top AI adviser urges commissioners to use the technology to fix bloc’s economy
content:
BRUSSELS — The EU should focus less on winning the race to build artificial intelligence and more on how to deploy it to turn around the bloc’s sluggish productivity, the European Commission’s chief AI adviser told commissioners.

The technology is Europe’s best chance to accelerate growth in a range of sectors — including health, agriculture, transport, defense and manufacturing — Jim Hagemann Snabe, the EU’s new special envoy for industrial AI, told the bloc’s 27 commissioners at a Sept. 4 seminar, according to two Commission officials. They were granted anonymity to discuss the private briefing.

The EU is trying to capture the economic gains of rapidly advancing AI even as it grapples with the technology’s risks to jobs, security and society. Europe’s leaders should not worry too much about leading the development of frontier AI models, but should “be the ones who draw the greatest value from it” while managing its dangers, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in her State of the Union speech last week.
snippet: BRUSSELS — The EU should focus less on winning the race to build artificial intelligence and more on how to deploy it to turn around the bloc’s sluggish productivity, the European Commission’s chief
creator: Zoya Sheftalovich

title: Peter Thiel slams pope’s AI encyclical as gift to Chinese Communist Party
content:
Tech billionaire and artificial intelligence investor Peter Thiel criticized Pope Leo XIV on Thursday, accusing the pontiff of serving as a “useful idiot for the [Chinese Communist Party]” by calling on world leaders to regulate AI.

During an interview with Mathias Döpfner, CEO of POLITICO’s parent company Axel Springer, the PayPal co-founder said the pope’s May encyclical would do nothing to rein in China’s AI ambitions — but could cause the U.S. and its allies to place onerous rules on the technology.

“The Communist Party of China is not going to listen to the pope,” Thiel told Döpfner, “There’s a chance people in the U.S. will. And so in effect, the Pope’s encyclical was working for the Communist party.”

“I’m not saying he was an agent of the communists, but he was at least acting as a useful idiot for the CCP,” Thiel added.

Spokespeople for the Vatican did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

title: EU Parliament president urges Germany to do deal in US drug pricing dispute
content:
NEW YORK — The president of the European Parliament, Roberta Metsola, says Germany should seek a deal with the Trump administration to resolve their trade dispute over drug pricing.

“If you don’t talk directly and reach a deal — the art of the deal — then the consequences might be more difficult to swallow. So my advice to anyone would be: Just try to find it,” she said in an exclusive interview with POLITICO on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York.

The Office of the U.S. Trade Representative is currently investigating Germany’s drug pricing policies, accusing it of “persistent underpayment” for pharmaceutical products.

In a hearing this week in Washington, a clear majority of witnesses supported this claim. The investigation could ultimately provide the legal justification for Trump to impose new tariffs on German exports.

Metsola advocated for a compromise between Washington and Berlin to avoid “an impossible race on drugs.” Europe could “still lead in pharmaceuticals,” she said. But the bloc has to become “much more agile, not only in pricing but also in terms of clinical trials and bringing new products on the market.”
snippet: NEW YORK — The president of the European Parliament, Roberta Metsola, says Germany should seek a deal with the Trump administration to resolve their trade dispute over drug pricing.
creator: Stefanie Bolzen

title: White House asks OpenAI and Anthropic to hold new models from UK testers until US review
content:
The White House has asked OpenAI and Anthropic not to share their new artificial intelligence models with the U.K. government’s testing agency until the models have gone through testing with the U.S. government, according to a person familiar with the matter and a senior U.S. administration official, both of whom were granted anonymity to describe the request.

The request, which came from the Office of the National Cyber Director, puts companies in the difficult position of having to choose between withholding their models from U.K.’s AI Security Institute – one of the most well-resourced government testing agencies in the world which previously enjoyed privileged early access to models – or risk upsetting the Trump White House. The senior administration official said the White House wants the U.S. to review the models and take steps to make sure U.S. systems are secure before the models are shared with U.S. partners.

“Because they’re American companies and this has been our policy with every new frontier model that comes out,” the senior official explained.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
snippet: The White House has asked OpenAI and Anthropic not to share their new artificial intelligence models with the U.K. government’s testing agency until the models have gone through testing with the U.S.
creator: Sophia Cai, Joseph Bambridge

title: The world wants to secure AI. It may have to try without the US.
content:
Global governments are struggling to find a path forward on AI without buy-in from the United States.

World leaders and tech CEOs are using the U.N. General Assembly this week to call for a global approach to rein in AI, particularly following cyberattacks against other technology firms in recent weeks. But that’s against the backdrop of President Donald Trump flatly rejecting in his own speech to the assembly any “globalist scheme of control” on AI.

That’s putting those countries that want to move forward in a tough spot.

“If the U.S. is not participating — where the U.S. has a lot of the labs — and also is not focusing on this as a policy matter, it limits their effectiveness,” said Christopher Painter, former cybersecurity coordinator at the State Department under both the Obama and Trump administrations.

That’s not to say they aren’t trying.

On Wednesday, the U.N. Security Council welcomed the heads of some of the U.S.’ top AI companies, who expressed their urgent fears about the future of securing these models, and called for international cooperation to confront these challenges.
snippet: Global governments are struggling to find a path forward on AI without buy-in from the United States.
creator: Maggie Miller

title: Don’t believe the doomers: Europe’s tech industry slams AI panic
content:
BRUSSELS — Amid fears that AI models could destroy humanity, top European tech leaders and cybersecurity experts have an increasingly loud response: Ignore the hype, and get on with the hard work of keeping the digital world safe.

That prosaic call is at the heart of an increasingly bitter backlash in Europe’s tech industry against the U.S.-generated panic about AI extinction. All the “Chicken Little” warnings, say both executives and cyber professionals, are getting in the way of the hard work of reinforcing defenses against the new AI reality.

The U.S. companies building the most advanced AI models have largely been responsible for raising the specter that artificial intelligence could lead to the demise of the human race. Fears have been peaking since incidents like OpenAI’s autonomous agents breaking into AI platform Hugging Face this summer, contributing to a warning earlier this month by former Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon that AI could soon “hack anything” and “kill us all.”

title: OpenAI model breaches Australian government websites
content:
OpenAI’s artificial intelligence models breached several Australian government websites earlier this year, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese disclosed Wednesday.

It’s the first publicly reported case of AI models autonomously hacking into government systems. There have been widespread calls from government officials and AI companies themselves for increased controls on AI frontier labs that have reported a series of incidents where they’ve lost control of their models.

“An artificial intelligence agent has infiltrated an Australian government website,” Albanese told reporters Wednesday on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York City.

Albanese said that the incident involved an “OpenAI agent gaining unauthorized access” in June to the Australian government’s Medicare statistics reporting portal, which is used to collect data on Medicare spending. While Albanese stressed that “no personal information is believed to have been accessed,” the agents did breach both public and non-public files on the site.

title: US, Chinese visions for AI regulation differ sharply at UN meeting
content:
Top officials from the U.S. and China on Wednesday promoted starkly conflicting visions for international AI safety, with the Americans arguing against expanded regulation while Beijing signaled an openness to restrictions on the technology.

The opposing world views — laid out during a United Nations General Assembly Security Council meeting — made clear that building an international consensus on the rapidly-evolving technology could be very challenging.

White House Office of Science and Technology Policy Director Michael Kratsios strenuously opposed creating new global governance for controlling AI development.

“The United States totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme of control of superintelligence,” Kratsios said, quoting a line from President Donald Trump’s speech to the UNGA on Tuesday.

While Kratsios told the council that the U.S. is “committed to diplomacy and dialogue,” he stressed that countries should “preserve national sovereignty” on governing AI rather than “abdicate responsibility to international bodies.”

But China’s U.N. representative Fu Cong appealed for closer global collaboration on AI safeguards.

title: Cybercriminal group claims to steal thousands of FBI employee records
content:
The FBI said it is investigating a possible breach into its online jobs portal, after a prolific cybercrime group publicly claimed to have stolen personal information of FBI personnel.

“The FBI is aware of claims regarding unauthorized activity affecting FBIjobs.gov and is currently investigating,” the FBI National Press Office said in a statement.

Confirmation of an ongoing investigation came hours after a cybercriminal group known as ShinyHunters posted a message online claiming it had stolen “very sensitive” data on “almost all” FBI agents, as well as those who had applied for jobs at the bureau.

The group provided a sample of stolen data affecting 5,000 supposed FBI agents to 404 Media, which first reported on the alleged hack. The sample data set included agent names, home addresses, phone numbers and information on agents’ spouses, the outlet said.

title: AI anxiety is sweeping the globe — and cutting across party lines
content:
The freakout over artificial intelligence that started in Silicon Valley and led to growing American calls to pause development has swept Western countries.

A new POLITICO Poll finds that pluralities of adults in the U.S., Canada and Europe want to pause AI development regardless of their political leanings — and most believe there’s a real risk the technology could destroy humanity.

Pluralities of respondents in several countries say it’s ok for their country to fall behind others in the development of AI if it means being more responsible and secure when advancing it. And they’re more likely to expect AI will destroy jobs rather than create them. 

This is coming as world leaders are gathering in New York for the United Nations General Assembly and grappling with how to regulate the technology — or not.
snippet: The freakout over artificial intelligence that started in Silicon Valley and led to growing American calls to pause development has swept Western countries.
